title: Wireless Communication
subtitle: WiFi with ESP32, Bluetooth LE, and LoRa for long-range IoT
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Physical sensor wiring doesn't scale — you can't run cables to every field sensor, wearable, or remote device. IoT requires embedded systems to communicate wirelessly over WiFi, Bluetooth, LoRa, or Zigbee.
whyItExists.solution: The ESP32 integrates dual-core CPU, WiFi 802.11 b/g/n, and Bluetooth 5.0 LE on a single $3–5 chip. It runs Arduino-compatible code and connects to cloud APIs, MQTT brokers, and home automation systems out of the box.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any IoT project needing wireless: smart home sensors, remote weather stations, wearables, WiFi-controlled devices, Bluetooth beacons.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Long cable runs in a building (use Ethernet for reliability). Safety-critical control systems (wireless latency is non-deterministic). Very-low-power battery devices with 10-year lifetimes (use LoRaWAN or Zigbee instead of WiFi).

explainModes.beginner: The ESP32 is a microcontroller with built-in WiFi and Bluetooth, like an Arduino that can connect to the internet. You can send sensor data to a website, receive commands over WiFi, or connect to your phone via Bluetooth — all from a $5 chip.
explainModes.simple: ESP32 connects to your WiFi router like a phone does. Once connected, you can make HTTP requests, run a web server, subscribe to MQTT topics, or send data to cloud platforms. It uses the same Arduino API so your existing knowledge transfers directly.
explainModes.standard: ESP32 (Espressif) uses a dual-core Xtensa LX6 at 240 MHz with 520 KB SRAM and 4 MB flash. The WiFi stack runs on Core 0, leaving Core 1 for application code. It supports WPA2, 802.11 b/g/n, AP and STA modes. BLE 5.0 uses GATT profiles.
explainModes.technical: ESP32 WiFi is interrupt-driven using the lwIP TCP/IP stack. HTTP calls via HTTPClient use TLS (mbedTLS). NVS (Non-Volatile Storage) stores credentials in flash encrypted partitions. ESP-NOW is a connectionless peer-to-peer protocol using WiFi MAC layer for <1ms, low-power device-to-device messaging.
explainModes.deepDive: ESP32 power modes: active (~160 mA), modem sleep (~20 mA WiFi off), light sleep (~0.8 mA), deep sleep (~10 µA, only RTC survives). Deep sleep + ULP (Ultra Low Power) coprocessor enables battery operation for years. WiFi consumes 160–300 mA during transmission bursts — alkaline batteries die quickly. Use LiPo + TP4056 charger or solar.

content.text: The ESP32: WiFi + Bluetooth on One Chip

The ESP32 from Espressif is the workhorse of modern IoT. It packs a 240 MHz dual-core CPU, 520 KB SRAM, WiFi 802.11 b/g/n, Bluetooth 5.0 LE, and 34 GPIO pins — all for $3–5. Install the ESP32 Arduino core via Board Manager: search for esp32 by Espressif.
HTTP Requests: Sending Sensor Data to an API
Once connected to WiFi, the ESP32 can make HTTP GET/POST requests using the HTTPClient library. Use this to push sensor data to REST APIs, home automation platforms, or cloud services.

The ESP32 can serve a web page over your local network — no cloud needed. Connect to the same WiFi and open the ESP32's IP address in a browser to control GPIO pins or view sensor readings in real time.

a.name: WiFi (ESP32)
a.useWhen: Indoor smart home, data-heavy sensors, devices near power outlets

b.name: LoRa (SX1276)
b.useWhen: Rural sensors, tracking, agriculture, long-range low-data-rate IoT

content.text: Store WiFi credentials in ESP32's NVS (non-volatile storage) using the Preferences library rather than hardcoding them. For production devices, implement a WiFiManager access-point setup mode so users can configure their own network without reflashing firmware.

ESP32 WiFi consumes 160–300 mA during transmission bursts. A standard 9V alkaline battery (~500 mAh) will last only ~3 hours in continuous WiFi mode. For battery-powered sensors, use deep sleep between readings — a 10-second wake cycle with 10-minute sleep reduces average current to ~15 µA, lasting months on a LiPo.

questions.question: What makes the ESP32 ideal for IoT compared to a standard Arduino Uno?
options: It includes built-in WiFi, Bluetooth, 240 MHz dual-core CPU, and 520 KB SRAM
It has a larger flash memory
questions.explanation: The ESP32 integrates WiFi 802.11 b/g/n, Bluetooth 5.0 LE, 240 MHz dual-core CPU, and 520 KB SRAM on one chip — none of which the Arduino Uno (16 MHz, 2 KB SRAM, no wireless) provides.

questions.question: Why is LoRa better suited than WiFi for a remote agricultural sensor in a field 5 km from the nearest building?
options: LoRa supports higher bandwidth for video streaming
LoRa has multi-kilometre range and very low power consumption — WiFi can't reach 5 km
LoRa uses the same 2.4 GHz band as WiFi
LoRa is cheaper than WiFi modules
questions.explanation: LoRa uses sub-GHz spread-spectrum radio reaching 1–10 km on a few milliamps average current. WiFi requires a router within ~50 m and draws 160+ mA — impractical for remote, battery-powered field sensors.

questions.question: What is ESP-NOW?
options: A connectionless peer-to-peer protocol for direct ESP32-to-ESP32 messaging without a router
questions.explanation: ESP-NOW is Espressif's proprietary protocol that enables direct peer-to-peer communication between ESP32/ESP8266 devices using WiFi MAC layer — no router needed, latency < 1 ms, and very low power overhead.

faq.q: What is the range of Bluetooth LE on ESP32?
faq.a: Typically 10–100 metres line-of-sight depending on antenna and obstacles. BLE 5.0 (supported by ESP32) extends range to ~200 m in open areas using long-range coded PHY. Good for local wearables, beacons, and mobile app control.

faq.q: How do I store WiFi credentials securely on ESP32?
faq.a: Use the Preferences library which writes to ESP32's NVS (Non-Volatile Storage) in an encrypted flash partition. For production, implement WiFiManager: ESP32 starts as an AP with a captive portal on first boot so the user enters their own credentials.

faq.q: My ESP32 keeps disconnecting from WiFi. How do I add auto-reconnect?
faq.a: Add `WiFi.setAutoReconnect(true); WiFi.persistent(true);` in setup(). Also check WiFi.status() periodically in loop() and call WiFi.reconnect() if it returns WL_DISCONNECTED. Use a watchdog timer (esp_task_wdt) for recovery if reconnect fails.
